Mi chiedo come sia la Romania
You ask indirect questions (mi chiedo se…, non so chi sia…, vorrei sapere dove…) with the indicative or the subjunctive, and talk about a trip to a new country and a Romanian wedding.
I don't know who he / she is
I wonder whether, who knows if
I wonder what Romania is like.
I don't know who told you that story.
I'd like to know if there are vampires in Romania.
I wonder if I'll like the food.
I was wondering why they steal the bride.
To ask yes / no indirect questions with "se": Mi chiedo se sia vero.
To use question words in indirect questions: Non so dove abiti.
To choose between the indicative (spoken) and the subjunctive (careful).
To apply the sequence of tenses: Mi chiedevo se fosse vero.
To use "chissà se" + future: Chissà se verrà.
To describe a trip and the wedding customs of another country.
24th April, the plane from Bologna to Sibiu. Graziella, who has never left Italy, is sitting by the window. Next to her are Pietro and Matei. Ion and Doina, of course, came by train.
I wonder what Romania is like. In seventy-two years I've never been out of Italy.
I'd like to know if there really are vampires in Romania.
(laughs) I don't know who told you that story, but the only vampire in Sibiu is my mother's dentist.
And I wonder if they'll understand my Romanian. I know three and a half words.
They'll ask you where you're from, how long you're staying and whether you've eaten. Above all, whether you've eaten.
And Radu? Do you know if he's written his wedding speech yet?
I don't know if he's written it. All I know is he's still scared of my father.
I wonder if I'll like the food. Doina says that at a Romanian wedding you eat for twelve hours.
It's true. And in the end you'll wonder how you managed to live seventy-two years without ciorbă.
Matei, can you explain why they steal the bride at midnight? Ilinca told me on the phone.
I'll explain tomorrow. Actually, no: tomorrow you'll see. And you'll wonder who invented it.
(looking out of the window) Matei… those mountains with the snow, what are they called?
They're the Carpathians. Welcome to my home.
"chi ti abbia raccontato" = who told you
A question you answer with "yes / no" becomes indirect with SE (= if, whether). After "se" you can use the indicative (spoken) or the subjunctive (careful):
Vorrei sapere se ci sono i vampiri.
I'd like to know if there are vampires.
I don't know if he's written it.
Mi domando se capiranno il mio romeno.
I wonder if they'll understand my Romanian.
The "se" of indirect questions is NOT the "se" of hypotheses. Here you can also use the future: "Mi chiedo se verrà" (I wonder if he'll come).
2. With question words: chi, dove, come, quando, perché
Mi chiedo come sia la Romania.
Non so chi te l’abbia raccontato.
Mi spieghi perché rubano la sposa?
In indirect questions there is NO inversion and no question mark unless the whole sentence is a question: "Non so dove abita.", NOT "Non so dove abita lui?".
Both are correct. The subjunctive is more elegant and expresses more uncertainty; the indicative is natural in speech:
After "dimmi", "spiegami", "ti dico" (when the answer is known) the indicative is used: "Ti dico io dov’è."
If the main verb is in the past, the subjunctive moves to the imperfetto (or trapassato):
I was wondering what Romania was like.
I didn't know who had told you.
Pietro wanted to know why they stole the bride.
5. Chissà se, chissà chi / dove / come
"Chissà" (who knows, I wonder) is a short indirect question, often with the future:
Who knows who invented this custom.
I wonder where Radu is now.
Can you explain why they steal the bride?
They'll ask you how long you're staying.
"I was wondering if it was true."
Dove vanno Graziella, Pietro e Matei?
Da quanti anni Graziella non esce dall’Italia?
Se in Romania ci sono i vampiri
Chi è «l’unico vampiro di Sibiu», secondo Matei?

Graziella had spent the whole journey wondering what she would find. She wondered whether Romanians were like Matei, kind and a little quiet, or like Ion, who talked about trains even to waiters. She wondered whether it would be cold, whether she would understand anything, whether she would get the presents wrong. When she came out of Sibiu airport, though, all the questions vanished at once. In front of her stood Doina, with a bunch of wild flowers and a sign written in Italian: "Welcome, my sister".

On the morning of the wedding, very early, Pietro made his first Romanian discovery: Lupu, Ion's dog, an enormous Carpathian shepherd dog with yellow eyes. Pietro stood stock-still for a minute, then asked Matei in a low voice whether it was a real wolf. "His name means 'wolf'," said Matei, "but he's better behaved than Totò." Ten minutes later Pietro and Lupu were running round the garden together, and nobody managed to separate them again.

The afternoon before, Matei had taken Graziella to the Brukenthal Museum. She wanted to know where the portrait was that everyone talked about, the one with the blue veil. When she found it, she stopped in front of the woman with Doina's eyes and asked Matei, almost in a whisper, whether it really was Grandma Viorica. "Nobody knows," Matei replied. "But my mother has decided it is, and in our family my mother's decisions count for more than documents." Graziella smiled and crossed herself.

The ceremony was in the great Lutheran church on the Great Square, with its pointed roof and bells you could hear all the way to the mountains. Graziella wondered why Romanians had a Lutheran church, and Matei had to explain eight centuries of Saxon history in five minutes. She nodded attentively, then said: "I didn't understand a thing, but it's beautiful."

Ilinca looked beautiful, in the white dress she had had made by a dressmaker in Mediaș, and Radu was so pale that Gennaro, who had arrived from Naples the night before, wondered whether he ought to keep a chair ready. The sponsors were a couple of doctors from Ilinca's hospital. When the pastor asked Radu whether he wanted to marry Ilinca, Radu first looked at Ion, as if asking his permission, and only then said yes.

The party was at a big restaurant outside the city, among the hills. Graziella didn't know what to expect, and she certainly didn't expect what she saw: tables thirty metres long, three hundred guests, a band with a violin, an accordion and a cimbalom, and a quantity of food she had never seen even in Naples. "I wonder who's going to eat all this," she said. At three in the morning she had her answer: everyone, and some people twice.

There was ciorbă, which Graziella tasted suspiciously and then ate three times. There were sarmale, which she already knew from Doina's lessons, but which were different here, smaller, cooked for twelve hours in a clay pot. There was cozonac, for which Graziella asked four different ladies for the recipe, each of whom gave her a different one, swearing it was the only true one.

At about eleven Radu stood up to give his speech. He had written it all on a sheet of paper, in Romanian and in Italian, because he wanted the guests from Italy to understand too. He thanked Ilinca's parents, then turned to Ion and said: "I still wonder how I had the courage to ask for your daughter's hand. But I know why I did it." Ion said nothing. He just raised his glass. And that was the best speech of the evening.

Then, at midnight, the thing Pietro had been waiting for for weeks happened. The lights went out for a moment, and when they came back on, the bride had gone. A group of Radu's friends had "kidnapped" her and taken her to another restaurant. Pietro was scandalised. "But why are they stealing her?" he asked everyone. "And who brings her back?" Matei explained that the groom has to pay a ransom, usually in bottles and songs, to get his bride back.

Gennaro, who knew nothing about the custom but understood the concept of organised chaos very well, immediately joined the kidnappers. In the end it was he who negotiated the ransom with Radu, in a mixture of Neapolitan, English and gestures: two bottles of pălincă, a Romanian song sung by Radu on his knees and a Neapolitan song sung by everyone. "We should do the same in Naples," he told Giulia when he got back. "Only with us, they'd never give the bride back."

At about three the last hora began. Graziella was sitting down, tired, when Ion came over and held out his hand, without saying a word. She wondered whether she could do it, but she had no time to think: a moment later she was in the circle, between Ion and Doina, spinning round and round, faster and faster, laughing like a young girl. Viola, in Matei's arms, was clapping in time, and Pietro was dancing with Lupu, whom someone had let in from the garden.

At dawn, as the band played the last song, Graziella went out onto the restaurant terrace. The hills were pink, the mountains in the distance still white with snow. Doina joined her with two cups of coffee. They stood there in silence, side by side, as they did in the kitchen in Florence, with no need for words.

In the end Graziella said, in Italian, knowing Doina wouldn't understand: "Do you know what I wonder? I wonder why I didn't come sooner. Seventy-two years, and I didn't know a place like this existed." Doina didn't understand the words. But she took Graziella's hand and replied in Romanian, knowing Graziella wouldn't understand: "Te întorci. Știu eu că te întorci." You'll come back. I know you'll come back.

Dear Franco, I'm writing to you from Romania! I wonder how I managed to live so many years without seeing this country.
Everyone asks me if I've eaten. I have. I've eaten an enormous amount. I don't know if I'll fit into my dress for the journey home.
